questions.question: What is an Application Load Balancer and at which OSI layer does it operate?
questions.answer: An Application Load Balancer (ALB) is a Layer 7 (Application Layer) load balancer that distributes incoming HTTP and HTTPS traffic across multiple backend targets. Because it operates at Layer 7, it can inspect the full HTTP request — including the URL path, headers, query strings, and HTTP method — and make intelligent routing decisions based on this content.

questions.question: What is path-based routing in an ALB?
questions.answer: Path-based routing is an ALB feature that routes incoming HTTP/HTTPS requests to different target groups based on the URL path. For example, requests to /products are forwarded to the products target group, /cart to the cart target group, and /orders to the orders target group. This enables a single ALB with one DNS endpoint to serve as the entry point for an entire microservices application.

questions.question: What is a Target Group?
questions.answer: A target group is a logical grouping of backend resources — such as EC2 instances, IP addresses, or Lambda functions — that receive traffic forwarded by a load balancer. Each target group has its own health check configuration and registers targets independently. The ALB only sends traffic to healthy targets within a group.

questions.question: What is an ALB Listener and what is a Listener Rule?
questions.answer: A listener is a process on the ALB that checks for incoming connection requests on a specified protocol (HTTP or HTTPS) and port (typically 80 or 443). A listener rule defines the routing logic: it specifies a condition (such as path is /products*) and an action (such as forward to the products target group). Rules are evaluated in priority order, and every listener must have a default rule as a fallback.

questions.question: What happens when all instances in a target group fail their health checks?
questions.answer: When all instances in a target group fail their health checks, the ALB has no healthy targets to forward traffic to. In this case, the ALB returns a 503 Service Unavailable error to the client. The ALB continues to run health checks and will resume sending traffic once an instance becomes healthy again.

questions.question: What is an Auto Scaling Group (ASG)?
questions.answer: An Auto Scaling Group is an AWS service that automatically adjusts the number of EC2 instances based on demand. You configure a minimum capacity (floor), maximum capacity (ceiling), and desired capacity (current target). ASG continuously monitors metrics via CloudWatch and scales out (adds instances) or scales in (removes instances) to maintain the desired state within those bounds.

questions.question: What is a Launch Template and why is it needed for an ASG?
questions.answer: A Launch Template is a blueprint that defines all the configuration needed to launch a new EC2 instance: the AMI, instance type, key pair, security groups, user data script, and more. ASG needs a launch template so it knows exactly what kind of instance to create when it scales out. Without it, the ASG wouldn't know what to launch.

questions.question: What are the three capacity settings in an ASG and what does each do?
questions.answer: The three settings are: Minimum capacity — the ASG will never run fewer instances than this value, even during zero traffic; Maximum capacity — the ASG will never exceed this number, preventing runaway costs; and Desired capacity — the current target that the ASG actively tries to maintain by launching or terminating instances as needed.

questions.question: What is the difference between ALB and NLB in terms of OSI layer and routing capability?
questions.answer: ALB operates at Layer 7 (Application Layer) and can route based on URL path, HTTP headers, query strings, and HTTP method — it reads the full HTTP request. NLB operates at Layer 4 (Transport Layer) and can only route based on IP address and TCP/UDP port — it never inspects the HTTP content. ALB is for intelligent web traffic routing; NLB is for ultra-low latency and non-HTTP protocols.

questions.question: Which load balancer supports Elastic IP (static IP) and why does it matter?
questions.answer: The Network Load Balancer (NLB) supports Elastic IP addresses, giving it a static, persistent public IP. The Application Load Balancer only provides a DNS name with dynamic IPs that can change. Static IPs matter when enterprise firewall rules whitelist specific IP addresses, or when clients need a fixed address to configure DNS or security rules.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to design a system that could handle different types of traffic to different backend services.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our monolithic application was being refactored into microservices — products, cart, and orders — each on separate EC2 instances. (Task) We needed a single entry point so clients didn't need to know about multiple backend addresses. (Action) I configured an Application Load Balancer with path-based routing: /products* forwarded to the products target group, /cart* to cart, and /orders* to orders. Each target group had its own health check path. (Result) The client only needed one DNS name, routing was transparent, and each service could be scaled or updated independently without affecting the others.

questions.question: Walk me through what happens when an ASG scales out and how the new instance starts receiving traffic.
questions.answer: (Situation) CPU utilization in our products service crossed 70% during a flash sale. (Task) The ASG needed to add instances without any manual intervention. (Action) CloudWatch detected the CPU alarm threshold breach and triggered the scaling policy. ASG used the products launch template to launch a new EC2 instance. Once the instance passed its initialization, it was automatically registered with the products target group. The ALB ran health checks against the new instance. (Result) Once health checks passed, the ALB began routing traffic to the new instance. The whole process took about 3-5 minutes with no manual steps and no dropped traffic.

questions.question: Describe how you would handle a client requirement for a static IP on a load balancer that also needs intelligent HTTP routing.
questions.answer: (Situation) An enterprise client needed to whitelist our load balancer's IP in their corporate firewall, but we also needed URL path-based routing for our microservices. (Task) ALB can't have a static IP, and NLB can't do path routing — we needed both. (Action) I implemented NLB → ALB chaining: an NLB at the edge with an Elastic IP (satisfying the firewall whitelist requirement), configured to forward TCP traffic to an ALB. The ALB handled HTTPS termination and path-based routing to the backend services. (Result) The client whitelisted a single static IP, and our routing rules worked exactly as designed. We got static IP from NLB and smart routing from ALB.

questions.question: How would you prevent a single point of failure in a target group?
questions.answer: (Situation) Our initial setup had one EC2 instance per target group. If it failed health checks, users got 503 errors. (Task) Eliminate the single point of failure. (Action) I attached an Auto Scaling Group to each target group with minimum capacity of 2, spanning at least 2 Availability Zones. This ensured at least one healthy instance was always available even if one AZ went down. I also tuned health check thresholds so transient blips didn't immediately remove healthy instances. (Result) The application maintained availability through AZ outages, instance failures, and deployments — users never saw 503 errors again.

questions.question: Tell me about designing a cost-efficient scaling strategy for a workload with predictable traffic patterns.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our SaaS application had consistent traffic spikes on weekday mornings (9am) and dropped significantly on weekends. (Task) Scale cost-efficiently without over-provisioning. (Action) I combined two scaling approaches: Scheduled Scaling to proactively scale up to 6 instances before 9am weekdays and scale down to 2 instances on weekends, plus Target Tracking Scaling (50% CPU target) to handle unexpected traffic spikes beyond the schedule. (Result) We reduced weekend and night EC2 costs by 60% while maintaining performance during peak hours. The combination of predictive scheduling and reactive target tracking handled all scenarios.

questions.question: A user reports intermittent 503 errors on your application. How would you troubleshoot?
questions.answer: (Situation) Users reported occasional 503 errors with no pattern. (Task) Identify root cause and resolve. (Action) I checked: (1) ALB access logs to identify which target group was returning 503s; (2) Target group health check status — found 1 of 3 instances was intermittently failing health checks due to a memory leak causing slow responses that exceeded the health check timeout; (3) CloudWatch metrics for the ASG showed the unhealthy instance was being cycled but the leak persisted. (Result) Fixed the memory leak in the application code and tightened the health check response timeout. Also increased minimum capacity so that one instance failure didn't reduce below acceptable serving capacity.

questions.question: How would you implement a blue-green deployment using ALB?
questions.answer: (Situation) We needed to deploy a new version of our API with zero downtime and the ability to instantly roll back. (Task) Design a deployment process with no traffic interruption. (Action) Created a 'green' target group with the new version's instances while the 'blue' target group served 100% of production traffic. Updated the ALB listener rule to switch traffic from blue to green instantly. Monitored error rates and latency for 15 minutes. (Result) If metrics were healthy, we kept green. If errors appeared, we updated the rule to switch back to blue in seconds. No downtime, instant rollback capability. We then terminated the blue instances after confidence was established.

questions.question: Describe a scenario where you'd choose NLB over ALB.
questions.answer: (Situation) A gaming company needed a backend load balancer for their real-time multiplayer game using UDP protocol with latency requirements under 10 milliseconds. (Task) Select the right load balancer. (Action) Chose NLB because: (1) the game used UDP, which ALB does not support; (2) NLB's ultra-low latency at Layer 4 met the <10ms requirement; (3) NLB provides a static IP for the game client SDK to connect to. (Result) NLB handled millions of UDP packets per second with consistent sub-millisecond routing latency. ALB would have been incompatible with UDP and introduced unnecessary HTTP parsing overhead.

questions.question: How does connection draining work and why is it important?
questions.answer: (Situation) During scale-in events, in-flight API requests were being dropped when ASG terminated instances, causing client errors. (Task) Eliminate dropped requests during termination. (Action) Configured connection draining (deregistration delay) on the target groups — set to 30 seconds for our API (short requests). When ASG selects an instance for termination, it first deregisters it from the target group. The ALB stops sending new requests but allows existing connections up to 30 seconds to complete. After 30 seconds (or when all connections close), ASG terminates the instance. (Result) Zero dropped requests during scale-in events.

questions.question: A new service needs to be added to the existing ALB microservices routing. Walk through the complete process.
questions.answer: (Situation) The team built a new recommendations service needing to be accessible at /recommendations. (Task) Add it to the existing ALB with no disruption to other services. (Action) (1) Launched EC2 instances for the recommendations service; (2) Created a new target group 'recommendations-tg' with appropriate health check on /recommendations/health; (3) Registered the instances with the target group; (4) Added a new listener rule: IF path is /recommendations*, THEN forward to recommendations-tg, with appropriate priority number; (5) Tested via the ALB DNS name. (Result) The new service was live with no downtime to existing /products, /cart, or /orders routing. One ALB serves all four services.

questions.question: An ALB has a listener rule matching /api*. A customer wants to route v1 and v2 of the API to different backends. How would you implement this without deploying a second load balancer?
questions.answer: ALB supports multiple conditions in a single rule, including query string conditions. You can create two rules: Rule 1 (priority 10): IF path matches /api* AND header 'Accept-Version' equals 'v2' → forward to api-v2-tg. Rule 2 (priority 20): IF path matches /api* → forward to api-v1-tg (catches all remaining /api traffic). Alternatively, use path-based versioning: /api/v1/* and /api/v2/* as separate conditions. This avoids deploying a second load balancer while achieving complete traffic isolation between API versions.

questions.question: Explain the architecture when you need an ALB behind an NLB and why this pattern is used.
questions.answer: The NLB → ALB chaining pattern is used when you need both a static Elastic IP and intelligent HTTP routing. NLB sits at the edge and is assigned an Elastic IP. The NLB target group uses IP type and registers the ALB's IP addresses (not DNS). NLB forwards raw TCP traffic to the ALB, which terminates TLS, reads HTTP content, and applies path-based routing rules. This is needed because ALB cannot be assigned an Elastic IP directly — its IPs are dynamic. The pattern gives you: (1) a static, whitelistable IP from NLB; (2) all HTTP routing capabilities from ALB.

questions.question: How would you handle Auto Scaling for a stateful application where each user session must stay on the same instance?
questions.answer: Stateful applications that require session affinity should use ALB sticky sessions (session persistence). Enable sticky sessions on the target group — the ALB generates a cookie (AWSALB) that binds a user to a specific instance for the session duration (configurable up to 7 days). However, this creates scaling challenges: when new instances are added via ASG, they receive less traffic initially since existing users stick to old instances. The better architectural approach is to externalize session state to ElastiCache or DynamoDB, making the application stateless and allowing true horizontal scaling. Sticky sessions should be a temporary measure, not the long-term solution.

questions.question: Design an Auto Scaling strategy for a batch processing system that receives massive jobs at random times and must process them quickly but idle cheaply between jobs.
questions.answer: This is a job-queue-driven scaling pattern using SQS as the trigger metric. Architecture: ASG with minimum=0 (yes, zero — no instances when idle), maximum=50. Scaling metric: SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible via custom CloudWatch metric. Target tracking policy targets 100 messages per instance. When a large batch arrives: SQS queue depth grows, CloudWatch alarm triggers, ASG scales from 0 to N instances using the launch template, instances process the queue using SQS polling, as the queue drains, instances scale in back to 0. Cost impact: zero EC2 cost when idle. Use Spot Instances in the launch template for additional 60-70% cost reduction on batch workloads that can tolerate interruption.

questions.question: What are the key differences in how ALB and NLB handle TLS/SSL termination?
questions.answer: ALB performs SSL termination at the load balancer — the ALB decrypts the HTTPS traffic, inspects the HTTP content to apply routing rules, then forwards unencrypted HTTP to backend instances (or re-encrypts with a separate certificate). This requires the SSL certificate to be installed on the ALB. NLB supports both TLS termination (similar to ALB) and TLS passthrough — where the encrypted connection passes through the NLB without decryption and is terminated at the backend instance. TLS passthrough preserves end-to-end encryption and is required for compliance environments (e.g., PCI-DSS) where decrypting at the load balancer is not allowed. ALB cannot do passthrough — it always terminates TLS.
